title: Coin Change
description: Fewest coins to make `amount`. Bottom-up dp[a] = min over coins of dp[a - c] + 1. Returns -1 if no combination reaches the amount.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me play it back: I have an array of distinct positive integers `coins` representing denominations, and a target `amount`. I want the *fewest* number of coins (with unlimited supply of each) that sum exactly to `amount`, or `-1` if no combination reaches it."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Unlimited supply of each coin, right? (As opposed to one-of-each — that's the 0/1 knapsack variant.)
• Are coins always positive, distinct integers?
• `amount = 0` — return 0 (zero coins needed)?
• Range — what's the upper bound on `amount`? (Affects whether `O(amount × coins)` is acceptable.)
• Return value — just the count, or also the actual coins used?
sections.why: The unlimited-supply question is *critical* — if it's one-of-each, the recurrence changes (you can't reuse `dp[a - c]` from the current pass, you'd need a 2D table or reverse iteration). The `amount = 0` clarification lets you anchor `dp[0] = 0` cleanly. The upper-bound question lets you preempt the 'is `O(amount × coins)` good enough?' pushback — for `amount ≤ 10^4` and a handful of coins, easily.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious exponential solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is recursive: `minCoins(a) = 1 + min(minCoins(a - c))` over every coin `c ≤ a`, with `minCoins(0) = 0` and `minCoins(negative) = Infinity`. Try every coin at every step, recurse on the remainder, take the best plus one. That's exponential — roughly `O(coins.length ^ amount)` — because the same subproblem `minCoins(7)` gets recomputed in countless branches (subtract 5 from 12, subtract 2 from 9 then 2 from 7, etc.). Massive overlap, perfect DP target."
sections.why: Two reasons to name it. (1) It's the natural framing — 'at each step pick a coin' is what an interviewer expects to hear first. (2) The overlap is the whole reason DP works here. Pointing out that `minCoins(7)` gets re-derived from many paths is what justifies caching, and the cache is exactly the bottom-up `dp` array.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to bottom-up tabulation?
sections.say: "This is 1D DP over the amount. The recurrence is `dp[a] = min over coins c of dp[a - c] + 1`, where `dp[a]` is the fewest coins that sum to `a`. The decision at each step is *which coin to use last* — and once you commit to coin `c` as the last one, the remaining problem is `dp[a - c]`, which is strictly smaller. So I build up from `dp[0] = 0` to `dp[amount]`, and for each subproblem I try every coin. Initialize the whole array to `Infinity` so unreachable amounts stay unreachable; at the end, if `dp[amount]` is still `Infinity`, return -1."
sections.why: Naming the recurrence in 'last coin used' framing is what makes it click. Saying 'min over coins' alone is too abstract; 'I'm asking what was the last coin — try each, the rest is a smaller subproblem' is the derivation. The `Infinity` sentinel is the trick that makes the unreachable case fall out of the same recurrence — no special-case branching for 'impossible'.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — the canonical case, an unreachable amount (returns -1), and a case where the greedy fails but DP wins.

examples.note: Unreachable — every odd amount stays at Infinity. The Infinity sentinel does the work.
examples.trace:
dp = [0, Inf, Inf, Inf]
a=1: c=2 > 1, skip. dp[1] still Inf
a=2: c=2 → dp[0]+1=1. dp[2]=1
a=3: c=2 → dp[1]+1 = Inf+1 = Inf. dp[3] still Inf
dp[3] === Infinity → return -1

examples.note: Greedy fails here — greedy picks 4+1+1 = 3 coins, but DP finds 3+3 = 2 coins.

sections.why: Tracing surfaces two important things. (1) The `[1,3,4] amount=6` case is the textbook reason DP beats greedy: greedy picks the largest coin first and gets stuck. (2) The `[2] amount=3` case validates the `Infinity` sentinel — `Infinity + 1 === Infinity`, so the propagation works without any guard clauses, and the final `=== Infinity → -1` check is the only special-case branch.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• `amount = 0` — `dp[0] = 0`, loop doesn't run, return 0. ✓
• Empty `coins` — every `dp[a]` for `a > 0` stays Infinity, return -1 for any positive amount. (Should clarify: do we even get empty coins?)
• `amount` smaller than the smallest coin — every coin is bigger, inner `if (c <= a)` skips, dp[a] stays Infinity. Returns -1.
• Coin value equals amount — `dp[a]` should be 1 via `dp[0] + 1`. Walked through it: works.
• Very large amount with small coins (e.g. coins=[1], amount=10000) — runs in `O(10000 × 1) = 10^4` ops, fine. The complexity is tight but the constant is small.
• Duplicate coins in the input — irrelevant for correctness (you'd just try the same coin twice per cell), but a dedupe would shave a tiny constant."
sections.why: The `amount = 0` case validates the seed without needing a guard — that's a senior signal, showing the recurrence's invariant is robust. The greedy-fail call-out (which you already made in section 4) is what justifies *why* this is DP and not a one-liner — interviewers often probe with 'why can't you just always use the biggest coin?'. Naming `[1,3,4] amount=6` as the counter-example is a clean rebuttal.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is `O(amount × coins.length)` — outer loop runs `amount` times, inner loop tries every coin, constant work per (amount, coin) pair. Space is `O(amount)` for the dp array.

The naive recursive version was `O(coins.length ^ amount)` — exponential. Memoization brings it to `O(amount × coins)` time / `O(amount)` space. Bottom-up tabulation keeps the same bounds with smaller constants (no recursion overhead).

For variants worth knowing: Coin Change II (count the *number of distinct ways* to make the amount instead of the minimum coins) — same `O(amount × coins)` shape, but you sum instead of taking min, and you iterate coins on the outer loop and amount on the inner to avoid double-counting permutations. The 0/1 knapsack (one coin of each) is also a small twist — iterate the amount in reverse to prevent reusing the same coin."
sections.why: Naming the `O(amount × coins)` bound with the exponential-to-polynomial trajectory is the defense — interviewers want to see you understand *why* DP saves you from the blow-up. The Coin Change II / 0/1 knapsack extensions prove you see the template family and know the loop-order trick (outer-vs-inner determines whether you count combinations or permutations). That same trick recurs in Combination Sum IV, Climbing Stairs Variant, and Partition Equal Subset Sum.

walkthrough.intro: Step through bottom-up Coin Change. The dp array fills left-to-right; each cell tries every coin and keeps the minimum. Infinity means "not reachable yet".
trace: const show = (arr) => arr.map(v => v === Infinity ? INF : v);
yield { line: 1, label: `enter — coins=${JSON.stringify(coins)}, amount=${amount}`, state: { coins, amount } };
yield { line: 3, label: `init dp[0..${amount}] = Infinity (unreachable)`, state: { coins, amount, dp: show(dp) } };
yield { line: 5, label: 'base: dp[0] = 0 (zero coins to make amount 0)', state: { coins, amount, dp: show(dp), lastFilled: 0 } };
tries.push(`c=${c}: dp[${a - c}]+1=${dp[a - c] === Infinity ? INF : dp[a - c]}+1=${cand === Infinity ? INF : cand}`);
yield { line: 10, label: `dp[${a}] = min over coins → ${dp[a] === Infinity ? INF : dp[a]}   [${tries.join(' | ')}]`, state: { coins, amount, a, dp: show(dp), lastFilled: a } };
yield { line: 13, label: `return ${dp[amount] === Infinity ? 'Infinity → -1' : `dp[${amount}] = ${dp[amount]}`}`, state: { coins, amount, dp: show(dp), returns: result } };

notes: Fill dp with Infinity so any unreachable subproblem stays Infinity and bubbles up to -1.
dp[0] = 0 anchors the recurrence — zero coins to make amount 0.
Unbounded coin supply means the inner loop reuses dp[a - c] from the SAME iteration (forward fill).
reference.crux: Ask which coin was used LAST: dp[a] = min over coins c of dp[a-c] + 1, seeded dp[0]=0; the rest (a-c) is a strictly smaller solved subproblem.
cruxDistractors: Greedily take the largest coin that fits, subtract, and repeat — fails on coins=[1,3,4], amount=6 (picks 4+1+1=3 instead of 3+3=2).
Recurse minCoins(a)=1+min over c of minCoins(a-c) with no memo — re-derives the same amounts exponentially.
dp[a] = dp[a-1] + 1 — assumes a coin of value 1 always exists and ignores the actual denominations.

alternates.label: BFS layer-by-layer (shortest path)
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer frames the problem as 'fewest steps' and you want to make the shortest-path lens explicit — treat each remaining sum as a node, coins as edges, and BFS depth IS the coin count. Often beats DP in practice because BFS short-circuits the moment it reaches `amount`, while bottom-up DP always fills the whole table.
notes: BFS guarantees the first time `sum === amount` we return is the minimum coin count — that's the shortest-path invariant in disguise.
The `visited` Set is load-bearing: without it the same partial sum gets re-expanded from every path that reaches it, blowing up to exponential work.
Often faster than bottom-up DP in practice — BFS exits as soon as it touches `amount`, while DP fills `dp[1..amount]` regardless of when the answer is found.

questions.q: The bottom-up recurrence for Coin Change is:
options: dp[a] = dp[a-1] + 1
dp[a] = min over coins c of dp[a-c] + 1
dp[a] = sum over coins of dp[a-c]
dp[a] = dp[a / 2] + 1

questions.q: Why fill the dp array with Infinity?
options: So `Math.min(dp[a], cand)` returns `cand` on the first valid coin instead of needing a special initial check
So unreachable amounts stay Infinity and convert to -1 at the end
So the dp array allocates as a packed Float64Array, which is faster than a sparse holey array
So `dp[a - c]` returns Infinity instead of undefined when `a - c` is out of bounds

questions.q: What does dp[0] represent and why is it 0?
options: It's a sentinel slot to detect off-by-one errors when the inner loop wraps around
Zero coins needed to make amount 0 — anchors the recurrence
It holds the smallest coin denomination, used as a tie-breaker in the inner min
It marks the array's lower bound so `dp[a - c]` returns 0 when `c === a`
O(amount)
O(coins.length)
O(amount * coins.length)
O(amount^2)
questions.explain: Outer loop runs `amount` times, inner loop tries every coin — O(amount * coins.length).

questions.q: Why does a greedy 'always take the largest coin' strategy fail? Take coins=[1,3,4], amount=6.
options: Greedy is too slow
Greedy picks 4 then 1+1 = 3 coins, but the optimum is 3+3 = 2 coins
Greedy returns -1 incorrectly
Greedy works fine here; it only fails on large inputs
questions.explain: Committing to the biggest coin first (4) strands you needing 2, costing three coins; DP explores all last-coin choices and finds the 3+3 two-coin optimum.

questions.q: What does dp[a] represent in this solution?
options: The number of distinct ways to make amount a
The fewest coins that sum exactly to amount a
Whether amount a is reachable (boolean)
The largest coin usable for amount a
questions.explain: dp[a] is the minimum coin count for amount a; the answer is dp[amount], or -1 if it stayed Infinity.

questions.q: The 'try each coin as the LAST coin used' framing makes each subproblem:
options: dp[a + c] — moving forward by one coin, which forces top-down recursion
dp[a - c], a strictly smaller amount — which is why bottom-up works
dp[c], the cost of making just the last coin's denomination (independent of a)
dp[a / c], dividing the remaining amount by the coin to skip already-counted multiples
questions.explain: Fixing coin c as the last one leaves the smaller amount a-c, so solving amounts in increasing order guarantees dp[a-c] is already final.

questions.q: Coin Change II asks for the NUMBER OF WAYS to make the amount. How does the recurrence change?
options: Nothing changes
You SUM dp[a-c] over coins instead of taking the min, and loop coins on the outside to avoid double-counting
You take the max instead of the min
You switch from DP to greedy
questions.explain: Counting ways accumulates (sum) rather than optimizing (min); iterating coins outermost counts combinations, not permutations.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the bottom-up Coin Change.

L3.prompt: Write `coinChange(coins, amount)` returning the fewest coins that sum to `amount`, or -1 if impossible. Log `coinChange([1, 2, 5], 11)`.
hints: Fill dp with Infinity, set dp[0] = 0.
For each amount a, try every coin c <= a; take min(dp[a], dp[a-c] + 1).
